summary: The Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator is a free, no-sign-up chemistry tool. Fill in the 2 fields it asks for and it works out mass of air straight away, with the formula shown underneath. It is built for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mass of air in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select a fuel); then you type in the air-fuel ratio (AFR) (2).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Mass of air=air-fuel ratio (AFR) × mass of fuel

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Select a fuel set to Methane (CH4), Air-fuel ratio (AFR) = 10 and Mass of fuel = 10 kg. Working through the relationship above gives Air-fuel ratio (AFR) = 10 and Mass of air = 100 kg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Air-fuel ratio (AFR) = 10 and Mass of air = 100 kg should be roughly the size you expected from Select a fuel set to Methane (CH4) and Air-fuel ratio (AFR) = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the air-fuel ratio (AFR) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mass of air, derived from the air-fuel ratio (AFR). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the air-fuel ratio (AFR), which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass of fuel in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass of fuel opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Air-fuel ratio (AFR) = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Air-fuel ratio (AFR) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
